# Exploratory Data Analysis

---

**Exploratory data analysis**, or **EDA** for short, can be thought of as a cycle:

-   Generate questions about our data.
-   Search for answers by visualizing, transforming, and modeling our data.
-   Use what we learn to refine your questions and/or generate new questions.

The main goal of EDA is to develop an understanding of your data. When we ask a question, the question focuses our attention on a specific part of the data set and helps us decide which graphs, models, or transformations to make.

-   EDA can be an intricate process that requires developing some keen investigation skills.
-   EDA can be creating one plot that tells a compelling story about the data.
-   [Exploratory Data Analysis with R](https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/exdata/){target="_blank"} by Roger Peng is a free textbook to help you dig deeper into EDA if interested!

# Tips for Good Graphics

---

Data graphics should be as *informative* as possible.

-   Graphics do *not* need to contain as much *information* as possible.
-   Make it as easy to understand the information you want to reveal about the data.
-   Simpler graphics are easier to understand and should be preferred.
-   Adding complexity to a graphic can sometimes reveal far more about the data than a simple graphic.
-   Make sure labels and text are large enough to easily read.
-   Make sure colors are distinguishable and colorblind friendly using the `viridis` color palette.

Complicated graphics may present far more information than we are able to process. You will have to decide what is needed in a graphic to make it as informative as possible.

# Choosing Colors

---

Choosing a color palette, line style, and/or shapes to represent the attributes with our plots can be very critical. Moreover, being able to choose visual aids that are accessible to individuals that see colors differently helps make your plots insightful for a general audience.


-   The traditional color palettes available in R are `rainbow`, `heat.colors`, `terrain.colors`, `topo.colors`, and `cm.colors`.

```{r}
#| echo: false
require("graphics")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

## color swatches for RGB/HSV palettes
demo.pal <-
  function(n, border = if (n < 32) "light gray" else NA,
           main = paste("color palettes;  n=", n),
           ch.col = c("rainbow(n, start=.7, end=.1)", 
                      "heat.colors(n)",
                      "terrain.colors(n)", "topo.colors(n)",
                      "cm.colors(n)")) {
    nt <- length(ch.col)
    i <- 1:n; j <- n / nt; d <- j/6; dy <- 2*d
    plot(i, i+d, type = "n", yaxt = "n", ylab = "", main = main)
    for (k in 1:nt) {
        rect(i-.5, (k-1)*j+ dy, i+.4, k*j,
             col = eval(str2lang(ch.col[k])), border = border)
        text(2*j,  k * j + dy/4, ch.col[k])
    }
}
demo.pal(16)
```

-   The `hcl.colors` palette function was added in R 4.0.0 and provides numerous excellent color palettes that are included in the appendix at the end of this module.
![hcl color palette](https://blog.r-project.org/post/2019-04-01-hcl-colors_files/figure-html/swatch-plot-1.svg)
-   Running the examples in the documentation found in `?grDevices::hcl.colors` will show examples of the available palettes through `grDevices`.
-   There are color swatches for many palettes in the appendices at the end of this module.
-   The [`colorspace`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/colorspace/vignettes/colorspace.html) package provides many of the same HCL palettes available through the `hcl.colors` palette, but it also provides convenient functions for accessing this in `ggplot2`.


# Example: Modeling HDI and Electricity Consumption Data

---

## About the HDI Data

---

The Human Development Index (HDI) data is from the [United Nations Development Programme](https://undp.org/) that oversees the calculation of HDI based on the following stated criteria:

> The Human Development Index (HDI) is a summary measure of average achievement in key dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, being knowledgeable and having a decent standard of living. The HDI is the geometric mean of normalized indices for each of the three dimensions.

HDI values are standardized scores from 0 (poor HDI) to 1 (perfect HDI). Data downloaded 3/8/2025 from <https://hdr.undp.org/data-center/human-development-index#/indicies/HDI>,

## About the Electricity Consumption Data

---

Electricity consumption data contains the electricity use per capita in kilowatt-hours per capita (kWh per capita) for all countries in the world (for which there is data) over the years 1960-2023 (though most countries last reported data in 2014). The data is from the [World Bank Databank](https://data.worldbank.org/). Data downloaded 3/8/2025 from <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/EG.USE.ELEC.KH.PC/countries>.


## Visually Exploring the Data 

---

First we import and expect the data.

```{r}

hdi_elec_all <- read_rds("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aspiegler/Applied-Regression/main/Data/hdi_electric.rds")
str(hdi_elec_all)
```

Let's filter out the data we want to work with.

```{r}
print(hdi_elec)
```

```{r}
# as electricity consumption goes up so does hdi
# but there is an outlier that makes it hard to see others
plot(hdi ~ electricity_use, data = hdi_elec)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# who is the outlier?
slice_max(hdi_elec, electricity_use, n = 5)
```



```{r}
# adding region to the plot
plot(hdi ~ log(electricity_use), 
     data = hdi_elec,
     col = region)
```



```{r}
#| warning: false
gghdi <- ggplot(hdi_elec, aes(x = log(electricity_use), y = hdi)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = income_group, shape = income_group), size = 2) +  # create scatter plot

gghdi
```

# Hawks Data

---

```{r}
hawks <- read_rds("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aspiegler/Applied-Regression/main/Data/hawks_clean.rds")
glimpse(hawks)
```


The data frame `hawks`has 908 observations on 19 variables. Some of the variables we will consider are:

- `species`: `CH` = Cooper's, `RT` = Red-tailed, `SS` = Sharp-Shinned
- `age`: 	`I` = Immature or `A` = Adult
- `sex`:	`F` = Female or `M` = Male
- `wing`:	Length (in mm) of primary wing feather from tip to wrist it attaches to
- `weight`:	Body weight (in g)
- `culmen`:	Length (in mm) of the upper bill from the tip to where it bumps into the fleshy part of the bird
- `hallux`:	Length (in mm) of the killing talon
- `tail`:	Measurement (in mm) related to the length of the tail (invented at the MacBride Raptor Center)
- `standard_tail`:	Standard measurement of tail length (in mm)
- `tarsus`:	Length of the basic foot bone (in mm)
- `wing_pit_fat`:	Amount of fat in the wing pit
- `keel_fat`:	Amount of fat on the breastbone (measured by feel)

# Numeric Summaries of Variables

---

- [See text section 2.3](https://jfrench.github.io/LinearRegression/data-cleaning-and-exploration.html#numerical-summarization-of-data)
- [See Statistical Theory Materials](https://aspiegler.github.io/Statistical-Theory/02-EDA-Categorical.html)


Numerical exploration of a data set generally consists of computing various relevant statistics for each of the variables in a data set in order to summarize the data.

| numeric summary  | variable type | summarizes        | R function            |
|------------------------|----------------|----------------|-----------------|
| mean             | `numeric`     | center  | `mean` |
| median           | `numeric`     | center | `median` |
| variance         | `numeric`     | spread  | `var`  |
| standard deviation  | `numeric` | spread  | `sd` |
| interquartile range  | `numeric`  | spread | `IQR` |
| quantiles        | `numeric`     | center and spread | `quantile` |
| correlation      | `numeric`     | similarity | `cor`  |
| frequency distribution  | `factor` | counts  | `table`|
| relative frequency distribution | `factor` | proportions | `prop.table` |

## The `summary()` Function

---

The `summary()` function is one of our favorite R commands by now. It provides a numerical summary for a single vector or for all columns of a data frame at once. The `summary()` function gives a different summary depending on the data type. For example, the output for `numeric` `factor`, or `character` variables are totally different.

```{r}
summary(hawks)
```


## Quantitative Variables

---

Numerical exploration of a set of quantitative (`numeric`) values usually focuses on determining the:

1.  center
2.  spread
3.  quantiles/percentiles
4.  correlation (between two different variables)


## Question 1

---

Use R commands to calculate the mean, median, and standard deviation of the culmen length of all hawks in the sample. Then interpret the practical meaning of these numerical summaries. Include units in your interpretation when possible.

::: {.callout-tip}
If you get an error message or output that does not make sense at first, you can access help documentation with commands such as `?mean` that might help you correct the error.
:::


### Solution to Question 1

---

```{r}
mean(hawks$culmen, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r}
median(hawks$culmen, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r}
sd(hawks$culmen, na.rm = TRUE)
```


The average culmen length is $21.8015$ mm. The median culmen length is $25.5$ mm. Thus, half of the hawks in our sample have a culmen length less than $25.5$ mm, and half have a culmen length greater than $25.5$ mm. Since the mean is less than the median, this means the data is skewed to the left (most values are on the right, but a tail of outliers exist on the left). There are some outliers with very small culmen lengths. 

The standard deviation is approximately $7.28$ mm. This roughly means the average distance of each culmen length to the mean culmen length is $7.28$ mm. The previous sentence may not sound to practical. We can informally say "many" of the culmen values are $21.8015$ mm $\pm 7.28$ mm, or "most" are between $21.8015$ mm $\pm 2(7.28)$ mm.


::: {.callout-note}
In the interpretation of the standard deviation, we roughly apply what is often called the 68%-95%-99.5% Rule or the *Empirical Rule* which says if a distribution is normally distributed then: 68% of the data is within $\pm 1$ standard deviation from the mean, 95% of the data is within $\pm 2$ standard deviations from the mean, and 99.5% of the data is within $\pm 3$ standard deviations from the mean. The less normal the data is distributed, the less accurate this rule becomes.
:::


## Question 2

---

Subset or slice the data into two different data frames:

- The data frame `immature` contains all columns for just the rows with `age` value equal to the `I`.
- The data frame `adult` contains all columns for just the rows with `age` value equal to the `A`.

Comment on how large the sample of immature and the sample of adult hawks are. Then calculate the $0.9$ quantiles for culmen length of the adult hawks and the immature hawks, separately. Interpret the values and comment on how the quantiles compare to each other.

### Solution to Question 2

---


```{r}
# subsetting the data
immature <- hawks[hawks$age == "I", ]  # using indexing and logicals
adult <- filter(hawks, age == "A")  # using dplyr
#adult <- subset(hawks, age == "I")  # using base::subset
```

```{r}
nrow(immature) # number of rows equals data frame is number obs
length(adult$age)  # length of a vector also gives number obs
```


```{r}
quantile(immature$culmen, probs = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE)
quantile(adult$culmen, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE)  # don't need to name probs arg, it is implied
```

There are a total of 684 immature hawks in the data and 224 adult hawks in the data. 90% of all immature hawks in the sample had a culmen length less than $28.7$ mm. 90% of all adult hawks in the sample had a culmen length less than $29.08$ mm. The 90th percentile for culmen length of adults is slightly ($0.38$ mm) higher compared to immature hawks. Intuitively it makes sense the immature hawks have smaller culmen lengths than adult hawks.


## Question 3

---

Find the five number summary for culmen length for the sample of adult hawks and the sample of immature hawks. Then interpret the practical mean of the five number summary of the immature hawks.


### Solution to Question 3

---

```{r}
summary(immature)
```


```{r}
# returns just the 5 numbers
# NA's are filtered out by default, yay!
fivenum(immature$culmen)
```

- The five number summary for culmen length of the immature hawks is $(8.6, 12.7, 25.7, 27.3, 34.1)$.

25% of all immature hawks in the sample have a culmen length between each pair of successive values in the five number of summary. In other words:

- One-quarter of the immature hawks in the sample have a culmen length between $8.6$ mm and $12.7$ mm.
- $25\%$ of the immature hawks in the sample have a culmen length between $12.7$ mm and $25.7$ mm.
- And so on.
- The middle 50% of the immature hawks in the sample have a culmen length between $12.7$ and $27.3$ mm.

::: {.callout-note}
The distance between the first and third quartiles, denoted $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ respectively, is called the **interquartile range** or **IQR**. It gives the width of the spread of the middle 50% of values in the data. In R, we can calculate the IQR with `IQR()`.
:::

```{r}
# comparing two methods
# need to specify to remove na
IQR(immature$culmen, na.rm = TRUE)

quantile(immature$culmen, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) - # Q3 -
  quantile(immature$culmen, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)  # Q1 
```


```{r}
# includes additional info
# NA's are also filtered out by default
summary(adult$culmen)
```

```{r}
# finding each value separately
min(adult$culmen, na.rm = TRUE)  # find minimum value
quantile(adult$culmen, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)  # Q1 = 0.25 quantile
median(adult$culmen, na.rm = TRUE)  # find minimum value
quantile(adult$culmen, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)  # Q3 = 0.75 quantile 
max(adult$culmen, na.rm = TRUE)  # find minimum value
```

- The five number summary for culmen length of the adult hawks is $(9.3, 12.95, 25.3, 27.5, 39.2)$.

### Notation and Terminology

---

- For a **sample**, we use $\bar{x}$ and $s$ to denote the mean and standard deviation, respectively. These are **statistics** since they summarize a sample.
- For a **population**, we use Greek letters $\mu$ and $\sigma$ to denote the mean and standard deviation. These are **parameters** since they summarize a population.
- When performing **statistical inference**, usually the values of the parameters are unknown, but we can estimate their values using statistics that we measure from a sample.
- Since there is randomness in the sampling process, estimates will vary from sample to sample, and we should build some **uncertainty** into our estimates.

For samples, we have the formulas


$$\bar{x} = \frac{x_1 + x_2 + \ldots + x_n}{n} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i}{n}$$
and 

$$s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}}.$$


### Correlation

---

The correlation between two `numeric` variables quantifies the strength and direction of their linear relationship.

The most common correlation statistic is Pearson's correlation statistic (or **correlation coefficient**). If $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ and $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ are two sets of `numeric` values, then the sample correlation statistic is computed as 

$$r = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{s_x}\right)\left(\frac{y_i - \bar{y}}{s_y}\right),$$

where:

-   $\bar{x}$ and $s_x$ denote the sample mean and standard deviation of the $x$'s.
-   $\bar{y}$ and $s_y$ denote the same thing for the $y$'s.

$r$ must be between -1 and 1.

The `cor` function can be used to compute the sample correlation between two `numeric` variables.

::: {.callout-note}
The typical convention of using Greek letters for population parameters and Latin letters for sample statistics applies to correlation. Namely we use $r$ for a correlation coefficient of a sample and $\rho$ for a correlation coefficient for population data.
:::

#### Interpreting the Value of the Correlation Coefficient

---

-   The closer $r$ is to $-1$ or $1$, the closer the data values are to a straight line.
-   $r$ values close to 0 indicate that there is no linear relationship between the two variables.
-   Negative $r$ values indicate a negative relationship between the two variables (as values of one variable increase, the values of the other variable tend to decrease).
-   Positive $r$ values indicate a positive relationship between the two variables (as values of one variable increase, the values of the other variable also tend to increase).

## Question 4

---

In the code below, we compute the sample correlation between the `wing` and `tail` variables in `hawks`. Notice the argument `use = "complete.obs"` is used to remove any observations with either a missing `wing` or `tail` value before calculating the correlation. Interpret the practical meaning of the correlation coefficient.


```{r}
#| eval: true
# determine whether each variable is numeric
cor(hawks$wing, hawks$tail, use = "complete.obs")
```

### Solution to Question 4

---

We see there is a positive association between `wing` and `tail` lengths of hawks. This makes sense since we'd expect as a hawk's `wing` length grows, its `tail` length would also tend to grow. The fact that the value is close to 1 means the association should be close to linear.  We expect a plot of the points to be approximately linear and going up with a roughly constant, positive slope.


## Question 5

---

Insert a code cell below to calculate the correlation between hawk `wing` and the `year`. Then interpret the value of the result. Does the result align or contradict your intuition?


### Solution to Question 5

---

```{r}
# determine whether each variable is numeric
cor(hawks$wing, hawks$year, use = "complete.obs")
```

The correlation coefficient is $r = -0.204111$. The value is negative which means there is a negative association between the variables. For example, as the time goes on (`year` increases) the `wing` lengths tend to get smaller. The value is close to 0 which there is not a strong linear association. We might expect a plot of the points to be more a cloud of data rather than see a pattern.



## Categorical (or Qualitive) Data

---


### Frequency Tables 

--- 

Tables of frequencies (or counts) are useful for determining how many observation are in each class of a categorical variable. We can use the `table()` function to get the distribution of frequencies.

```{r}
# table function returns counts for one variable
table(hawks$age)  # na values removed by default
```


### Contingency (Two-Way) Tables 

--- 

A **contingency table** (or **two-way table**) gives the number of observations in BOTH a specified class of one variable AND another specified class of a second variable.

## Question 6

---

Run the code cell below to generate a two-way that shows the relationship between the `age` and `species` variables. Which species has the most adult hawks? Which species has the most immature hawks?

```{r}
# table function returns two-way table to compare 2 categorical variables
table(hawks$age, hawks$species)
```

### Solution to Question 6

---

The red-tailed species has both the most adult hawks (454) and the most immature hawks (123) in the sample.


### Relative Frequency Tables

---

A **relative frequency table summarizes** the proportion or percentage of observations with each level of a categorical variable. 

::: {.callout-note}
Relative frequencies typically provide more context and are more meaningful when comparing data that is not uniformly distributed. When some classes have a lot of observations and others few, comparing counts can be misleading.
:::

One convenient way to construct a relative frequency table is to apply the `prop.table(tbl)` to a table previously stored in `tbl`. From the output of the `prop.table()` function below we see $24.67\%$ of the values in `hawks` are from adults and the other $75.53\%$ of the values are for immature hawks.


```{r}
my_tbl <- table(hawks$age)
my_tbl
```

```{r}
prop.table(my_tbl)
```


### Joint Distributions and Marginal Distributions

---

When we apply the `prop.table(two_way_tbl)` function to a two-way table stored in `two_way_tbl`, the output tells us what proportion of all observations in the data frame are both a specified class of one variable and a specified class of a second variable. **By default the proportions are calculated relative to the grand total**. In other words, we divide each of the counts in `two_way_tbl` by the total number of all observations. The resulting table gives the  **joint distribution** for variables `age` and `species`.

```{r}
# table function returns two-way table to compare 2 categorical variables
two_way_tbl <- table(hawks$age, hawks$species)
two_way_tbl
```

```{r}
# proportions relative to grand total
prop.table(two_way_tbl) |> 
  round(4)  # pipe output into round function to round to 4 decimal places
```

```{r}
# manually divide each count by total number of observations
# returns same result
round(two_way_tbl / nrow(hawks), 4)  
```

We can compute the relative frequencies relative to either the row totals or the columns totals by adding the option `1` or `2` after entering the table.

- Adding the option 1, `prop.table(two_way_tbl, 1)`, gives proportions relative to the row totals. 
  - Each count in `two_way_tbl` is divided by the total count in each row.
  - The sum of the proportions in each row should add up to 1.
  - In our example below, we each proportion is relative to the total number in each `age` group (each row is a different `age` group.)
  

```{r}
# adding option 1 to prop.table()
prop.table(two_way_tbl, 1) |>  # proportions are relative to row totals
  round(4)  # round to 4 decimal places
```

- Adding the option 2, `prop.table(two_way_tbl, 2)`, gives proportions relative to the column totals. 
  - Each count in `two_way_tbl` is divided by the total count in each column.
  - The sum of the proportions in each column should add up to 1.
  - In our example below, we each proportion is relative to the total number in each species (each column is a different `species`.)
  

```{r}
# adding option 2 using pipe
table(hawks$age, hawks$species) |>  # first find two-way table (not stored)
  prop.table(2) |>  # then convert to prop relative to col totals
  round(4)  # finally round to 4 decimal places
```

## Question 7

---

Based on the output from the three different `prop.table()` (relative to grand total, row totals, and column totals), answer the following questions and indicate which table was most useful at answering the question.

- If an adult hawk in the sample is randomly selected, which species is the hawk most likely?
- If a Cooper's hawk in the sample is randomly selected, which age group is it mostly likely in?
- Which species has the greatest proportion of adults hawks in its sample?

### Solution to Question 7

---

- If an adult hawk in the sample is randomly selected, it is mostly likely to be a Red-tailed species of hawk. We can see in from the output of `prop.table(two_way_tbl, 1)` that there is a $54.91\%$ chance it is a red-tailed hawk compared to $14.29\%$ (for Cooper's) and $14.29\%$ (for Sharp-shinned).

- If a Cooper's hawk in the sample is randomly selected, it is mostly likely to be an immature hawk. We can see in from the output of `prop.table(two_way_tbl, 2)` that there is a $54.29\%$ chance it is immature compared to a $45.71\%$ chance it is adult.

- Cooper's hawks have the greatest proportion of adults within their sample. We can see in the output from `prop.table(two_way_tbl, 2)` that $45.71\%$ of the Cooper's hawks are adult compared to $21.32\%$ and $26.44\%$ for Red-tailed and Sharp-shinned hawks, respectively.



# Visual Summaries of Data

---

Visual summaries (i.e., plots) of data help us:

-   Spot errors in our data, unusual observations, and simple patterns.
-   Communicate the results of our analysis.

The two most popular packages for producing graphics in R are:

-   `base`: the default graphics system
-   `ggplot2`: a "grammar of graphics" that is able to produce complex graphics with automated legends in a consistent, systematic way.


| Visual summary | Variable types  | Summary type | Base functions| geoms  |
|:--------------|:--------------|:--------------|:--------------|:--------------|
| box plot  | 1 `numeric`| univariate   | `boxplot(x)`     | `geom_boxplot`|
| histogram  | 1 `numeric`| univariate   | `hist(x)`        | `geom_histogram`|
| density plot   | 1 `numeric`| univariate   | `plot(density(x)` | `geom_density`|
| bar plot   | `factor` | univariate   | `plot(x)` or `barplot(tbl)` | `geom_bar`    |
| scatter plot   | 2 `numeric` | bivariate  | `plot`  | `geom_point`  |
| side-by-side box plots   | 1 `numeric`, 1 `factor` | bivariate  | `plot(x, y)` or `boxplot(x, y)` | `geom_boxplot`|
| stacked or grouped bar plot   | 2 `factor` | bivariate  | `boxplot(prop.table(two_way_tbl))` | `geom_boxplot` |
| grouped scatter plot | 2 `numeric`, 1 `factor` | multivariate | `plot` | `geom_point`  |
| faceted plots | mixed | multivariate | none | `facet_wrap` or `facet_grid` |
| interactive plots | mixed | multivariate | none | `plotly::ggplotly`  |



## Using the Generic `plot()` function

---

The base R function `plot()` is the most generic plotting function, and it often does a pretty nice job of getting the ball rolling. Based on the data type and number of of the variables included, R will take an educated guess as to what plot might help visualize features of the data.

- If `fac` is a `factor`, then `plot(fac)` gives a **bar plot**.
- If `num` is a `numeric`, then `plot(num)` gives an **index plot** which is often not helpful.
- If `num` is a `numeric` and `fac` is a `factor`, then `plot(fac, num)` gives **side-by-side box plots**.
- If `num1` and `num2` are two `numeric` vectors, then `plot(num1, num2)` gives a **scatter plot**.
- If `fac1` and `fac2` are two `factor` vectors, then `plot(fac1, fac2)` is **not useful**.


### One Categorical Variable: Bar Plots

---

Factors such as `species` are plotted using a bar plot which is very reasonable.

```{r}
# a factor variable results in bar plot
plot(hawks$species)
```

- Run `?plot()` to see a list of arguments that can be added to the command. Below are some common arguments.
- A `legend()` can also be added to output of a `plot()`. Options are similar to `plot()`. Run `?legend()` for more info.


```{r}
plot(hawks$species,
     main = "Distribution of Hawk Species",  # main title
     xlab = "Species",  # title on x-axis
     ylab = "Count",  # title on y-axis
     col = c("red", "blue", "green"))  # fill colors

# add a legend to plot
legend(x="topright",  # place legend in top right
       legend = c("Red-tailed", "Cooper's", "Sharp-shinned"),  
       fill = c("red", "blue", "green"))  # use same fill colors
```


### One Numeric Variable: Index Plot

---


Numeric variables such as `culmen` are plotted using an index plot which is typically not very useful. Thus, we typically use other functions to plot one numeric variable in most situations. 

```{r}
plot(hawks$culmen)
```

## Question 8

---

Even though the index plot generated by `plot()` is not necessarily the best plot to identify key characteristics, can you identify any patterns or properties in the `culmen` measurements? If so, give a possible reason for observing the pattern.

### Solution to Question 8

---

There seems to be 2 or 3-ish bands of data. There are two clear bands and maybe a third, less dense band of points in the middle. Hard to tell if that is a third cluster or a transition between 2 without further analysis. These bands of points might represent different clusters of culmen lengths based on age band (immature or adult which could be two clusters) and/or species (RT, SS, and CH might be three clusters).

<br>  
<br>  


### Comparing One Numeric and One Categorical Variable: Side-by-Side Box Plots

---

Entering one categorical (factor) `df$fac` and one quantitative variable `df$num` into the generic `plot(df$fac,  df$num)` results in a side by side box plots. One box plot for each class of the categorical variable. This is a very fine choice by R!

```{r}
plot(hawks$species, hawks$culmen)
```

::: {.callout-note}
In the plot below we make use of the topo color palette that is available in `base` R.
:::


```{r}
plot(hawks$species, hawks$culmen, 
     main = "Distribution of Culmen Lengths by Hawk Species",  # main title
     xlab = "Species",  # title on x-axis
     ylab = "Culmen Length (in mm)",  # title on y-axis
     col = topo.colors(3))  # fill colors

# add a legend to plot
legend(x="topright",  # place legend in top right
       legend = c("Red-tailed", "Cooper's", "Sharp-shinned"),  
       fill = topo.colors(3))  # use same fill colors
```


## Question 9

---

Based on the plot generated by the previous code chunk, do you believe there is a relation between `species` and `culmen` length? If so, summarize the relation.

### Solution to Question 9

---

Yes. The three box plots have very different distributions of culmen lengths. The red-tailed have longest overall, followed by Cooper's, and lastly sharp-shinned hawks have the smallest culmen length overall of the three species. We can comment on any number of properties more specifically to support this conclusion.

- Comparing medians: The RT have largest median followed by CH and SS.
- Comparing other quartiles: About 75% of all RT have a culmen length greater than 25 mm while essentially all CH and SS have culmen lengths less than 25 mm (each have only one hawk outlier in each sample with a culmen length greater than 25 mm). Similarly about 75% of all CH have a culmen length greater than 16 mm will SS have only a handful of outliers with a culmen length greater than 16 mm.

Comparing spreads, we see the RT has the smallest interquartile range and the largest range. This means the middle 50% of RT have culmen lengths very close the median which is approximately 27 mm, but there are a lot of outliers spread equally on both the small and large end. CH are the reverse, they have the largest interquartile range and the smallest range. This means the middle 50% of CH have a relatively big spread (compared to SS and RT), but there is only one outlier, so tails on each end are not long.

Comparing shapes, the distribution of culmen lengths for RT is approximately symmetric. CH have a slight skew to the right. SS have a stronger skew to the right.

<br>  
<br>  

### Comparing Two Numeric Variables: Scatter Plots

---

**Scatter plots** can be used to examine the relationship between two `numeric` variables. Entering two numeric variables into the generic `plot(x, y)`results in a scatter plot which is totally reasonable! 

- The values from the first vector are plotted on the horizontal axis.
- The values from the second vector are plotted on the vertical axis. 
- Each observation is a single point associated with an ordered pair of values.
- The two vectors must have the same length.

```{r}
plot(hawks$wing, hawks$tail,
     main = "Association of Wing and Tail Lengths of Hawks",  # main title
     xlab = "Wing Length (in mm)")  # title on x-axis
```


We can also adjust the syntax of the `plot()` function to enter the information as `plot(y ~ x, data = df)`. Notice first we enter the response variable `y` which is plotted on the vertical axis and then the predictor variable `x` which is plotted on the horizontal axis. In this example:

- The response variable is the `numeric` variable, `tail`.
- The predictor variable is the `numeric` variable, `wing`.
- The `data` is `hawks`.

```{r}
# use the syntax boxplot(response ~ predictor, data = df)
plot(tail ~ wing, data = hawks)
```

### Comparing Two Categorical Variables: Stacked and Grouped Bar Plots

---

Entering two categorical (factor) variables into the generic `plot()` function does not work very unfortunately. We can create nice visual displays for comparing two categorical variables with the base R `barplot()` function and using the `ggplot2` package. Both methods are discussed shortly.


```{r}
plot(hawks$species, hawks$age)
```


## Base R Plotting Functions

---

The generic `base` R `plot()` function changes the type of plot based on the data types of the vectors that are input. There are additional `base` R plotting functions available that can create more customized plots. Below are some additional functions we'll explore:

- `barplot(tbl)` creates a bar plot based on summary stored in `tbl`, including grouped and stacked bar plots if `two_way_tbl` is input.
- `hist(x)` creates a histogram.
- `plot(density(x))` creates a density plot.
- `boxplot(x)` creates box plots (single or side-by-side)

### One Categorical Variable with `barplot()`

---

We can also convert a frequency table into a bar plot using the `barplot(tbl)` function. This illustrates the different sizes of the samples.

::: {.callout-caution}
The `barplot()` function must take a table as the input and not a vector. Thus, you must first create a frequency table and then input that table into the `barplot()` function.
:::


```{r}
# composing functions
barplot(table(hawks$species))
```

- The pipe is a nice way to compose operations.

```{r}
# composing actions with the pipe
table(hawks$species) |> 
  barplot()
```

- Run `?barplot()` to see a list of arguments that can be added to the command. Below are some common arguments.
- A `legend()` can also be added to output of a `plot()`. Options are similar to `barplot()`. Run `?legend()` for more info.

```{r}
# composing actions with the pipe
table(hawks$species) |> 
  barplot(main = "Distribution of Hawk Species",  # main title
          xlab = "Species",  # title on x-axis
          ylab = "Count",  # title on y-axis
          col = terrain.colors(3))  # fill colors)

# add a legend to plot
legend(x="topright",  # place legend in top right
       legend = c("Red-tailed", "Cooper's", "Sharp-shinned"),  
       fill = terrain.colors(3))  # use same fill colors
```


### Comparing Two Categorical Variables with `barplot()`

---

The generic `plot()` function creates a fine looking bar plot when we enter one categorical variable. To compare two categorical variables, the plot was not very useful. Instead, if we create and store a two-way table to `two_way_tbl`, the command  the `barplot(two_way_tbl)` will generate a **stacked bar plot**. 

- The second (column) variable `y` entered in `table(x, y)` will have each class plotted with different colors stacked on top of each other. The first (row) variable `x`  will have one bar (with multiple colors) for each class of `x` along the horizontal axis. 
- If we include the argument `beside = TRUE`, then we get a **clustered or grouped bar plot**.
- If we enter a table of proportions, `barplot(prop.table(two_way_tbl))`, we get relative frequency bar plots that give proportions instead of counts.
- By including the option `1` and `2` in `prop.table()`, we can adjust the totals out of which the proportions are calculated (grand, row, or column totals).


```{r}
# age on horizontal axis
# different colors stacked for each species
table(hawks$species, hawks$age) |>  # create frequency table
  barplot()  # construct bar plot of counts
```


::: {.callout-note}
The `hcl.colors` function provides has many additional color palettes. See the appendix for a more complete picture. In the code cell below, we use the `viridis` color palette which is the recommended choice for accessibility.
:::


```{r}
# convert to relative frequencies
num_species <- nlevels(hawks$species)  # nlevels() counts number of levels of species

table(hawks$species, hawks$age) |>  # species are rows and age is column
  prop.table() |>  # compute table of proportions relative to grand total
  barplot(col = hcl.colors(num_species, palette = "viridis"))  # change color of bars 
```

```{r}
# adding a legend
#num_species <- nlevels(hawks$species)  # nlevels() counts number of levels of species

table(hawks$species, hawks$age) |> 
  prop.table() |>
  barplot(col = hcl.colors(num_species, palette = "viridis"))  

legend(x="topleft",  # place legend in top left
       legend = c("Red-tailed", "Cooper's", "Sharp-shinned"),  
       fill = hcl.colors(num_species, palette = "viridis"))  # use same fill colors
```


```{r}
#num_species <- nlevels(hawks$species)  # nlevels() counts number of levels of species

table(hawks$species, hawks$age) |> 
  prop.table(1) |>  # prop relative to row (species) totals
  barplot(col = hcl.colors(num_species, palette = "viridis")) 

legend(x="topleft",  # place legend in top left
       legend = c("Red-tailed", "Cooper's", "Sharp-shinned"),  
       fill = hcl.colors(num_species, palette = "viridis"))
```

::: {.callout-caution}
In the plot above, the proportions stacked above the immature age group `I` add up to a value greater than 1 which is suspicious for proportions. The command `prop.table(1)` means the proportions are computed relative to the row variable which is species in this case. 

- The first rectangle in purple in the `I` stack has height $0.79$ which means $79\%$ of all Red-tailed hawks in the sample are immature. 
- Similarly, the green block has height $0.54$ which means $54\%$ of Cooper's Hawks are immature.
- The yellow block has height $0.74$, so $74\%$ of Sharp-shinned hawks are immature.
- Adding the values together gives a total height of approximately $2.07$
:::

The stacked relative frequency bar plot below is likely a more helpful display since all proportions are relative to each class plotted across the horizontal axis. Thus, the each stack has a height that adds up to one.


```{r}
table(hawks$species, hawks$age) |> 
  prop.table(2) |>  # prop relative to column (age) totals
  barplot(col = hcl.colors(num_species, palette = "viridis"))  # change color of bars 

legend(x="bottomright",  # place legend in bottom right
       legend = c("Red-tailed", "Cooper's", "Sharp-shinned"),  
       fill = hcl.colors(num_species, palette = "viridis"))
```

### One Numeric Variable

---

The generic `base` R `plot()` function will create an index plot with one numeric variable which is often not the best plot for exploring patterns in our data. Histograms, density plots, and/or box plots are better for performing initial data exploration on a single `numeric` variable.

#### Histograms

---

A  **histogram** is special bar chart we use to display the distribution of values for a quantitative variable.

-   We first group the values into different ranges of values called **bins** of equal width.
    -   This essentially converts the quantitative variable to an ordinal categorical variable with with each bin representing a different level.
-   The height of the bars over each bin range is the number of values (or frequency) in each bin range.
-   **By default, the counts are right closed.** For example, an HDI value of 0.5 knots would be counted in the bin range 0.4-0.5 and not counted in the bin range 0.5-0.6.
-   **The R function `hist(x, [options])` creates a histogram.**
-   Run `?hist` for more information about the available options for customizing a histogram, some of which are illustrated in the code cell below.


```{r}
hist(hawks$culmen)
```

```{r}
hist(hawks$culmen,  # vector of values to plot
     breaks = 15,  # number of bin ranges to use
     xlab = "Culmen Length (in mm)",   # x-axis label
     xlim = c(5, 40),  # sets window for x-axis
     ylab = "Frequency",  # y-axis label
     ylim = c(0, 250),  # sets window for y-axis
     main = "Distribution of Culmen Lengths",  # main label
     col = "steelblue")  # fill color of bars
```


```{r}
#| eval: true
# a relative frequency histogram
hist(hawks$culmen,
     freq = FALSE,  # relative frequency hist
     breaks = 20,
     xlab = "Culmen Length (in mm)",
     xlim = c(5, 40), 
     ylab = "Relative frequncy per mm",  # y-axis label
     main = "Distribution of Culmen Lengths",  # main label
     col = "steelblue")  # fill color of bars
```

#### Density Plots

---

A **density plot** is similar to a smoothed relative frequency histogram.

- The total area under the smoothed curve must equal 1.
- We typically read density plots by approximating the proportion of the total area that lies above a given range of values.
- We need to be careful how we interpret the height, so most people don't bother!
- On a more surface level, we can identify what seems to be a **bimodal** pattern in the distribution which might be attributed to other **lurking variables**.

We combine the `plot` and `density` functions to construct a density plot using `base` R.


```{r}
plot(density(hawks$culmen, na.rm = TRUE),
     col = "blue")
```



#### Box Plots

---

Box plots are another common and useful way to visually represent numeric data and identify . They are particularly useful for identifying outliers and skewness. However, we do lose detail and information (compared to histograms). 

If we align the box plot horizontally:

- A vertical line is drawn at each value in the five number summary. The length of each line should be the same and does not communicate any information.
- Form a rectangle by connecting the top and bottom of the vertical lines corresponding to $Q_1$ and $Q_3$. 
  - The median is indicated by the vertical line inside the rectangle.
  - The width of the rectangle equals the interquartile range.
- Extend a horizontal line from the middle of the vertical lines through the minimum to the middle of the vertical line corresponding to $Q_1$.
- Extend a horizontal line from the middle of the vertical lines through the minimum to the middle of the vertical line corresponding to $Q_3$.
- If there are outliers on either side, the process is modified slightly and outliers are indicated with dots.

The `boxplot(x)` function is the easiest approach for producing a single box plot using `base` R.


```{r}
boxplot(hawks$culmen, 
        main = "Distribution of Culmen Length for Hawks",
        horizontal = TRUE)
```



### Side-by-Side Box Plots with `boxplot()`

---


By default, if `fac` and `num` are a `factor` and `numeric` variable, respectively, then `plot(num, fac)` or `plot(fac ~ num, data = df)` will construct side-by-side box plots. When can also create side-by-side box plots using the `base` R `boxplot()` function that we used to create a single box plot. However, we will need to adjust the syntax since:


```{r}
# this does NOT give the desired result
boxplot(hawks$wing, hawks$species)
```


```{r}
# this does NOT give the desired result
boxplot(hawks$species, hawks$wing)
```

We use similar syntax as we used when creating a scatter plot with the generic `plot()` function, namely `boxplot(response ~ predictor, data = df)`. Notice first we enter the response variable which is a `numeric` plotted on the vertical axis. Then after the `~` we enter the the predictor variable which is a `factor` plotted separately across the on the horizontal axis. In this example:

- The response variable is the `numeric` variable `wing`.
- The predictor variable is the `factor` variable `species`.
- The `data` is in `hawks`.

```{r}
# use the syntax boxplot(response ~ predictor, data = df)
boxplot(wing ~ species, 
        data = hawks, 
        horizontal = TRUE,  # change layout direction
        col = hcl.colors(3, palette = "plasma"))  # using plasma palette
```

# Using `ggplot2` from the `tidyverse`

---


Thus far, we have created some perfectly fine looking visualizations in base R using function such as `plot()`, `hist()`, `boxplot()`, and `barplot()`. There are other plotting functions and packages in R that can be used to generate similar and additional plots.


Next we discuss how to perform basic data visualization use an R package called **ggplot2** (Wickham 2016; Wickham et al. 2023) which is perhaps the most powerful and intuitive package for producing data visualizations. `ggplot2` is different from most other graphical packages since it has a natural underlying grammar. In fact, that is what the `gg` in `ggplot2` stands for, namely *Grammar of Graphics*.  `ggplot2` is perhaps the most popular and powerful tool for constructing statistical graphics because it is so flexible and it has such an elegant framework.



## The Grammar of Graphics

---

Wilkinson derived the **grammar of graphics** to describe inherent properties foundational to all statistical graphics. The layered grammar of graphics developed by Wickham builds on Wilkinson's grammar, has been adapted for embedding within R, and has evolved into `ggplot`. A first description of the basic ingredients of `ggplot2` are described below. We first introduce new  terminology that we will develop further as we dig deeper into working with the `ggplot2` package.

There are 4 main components needed to produce a graphic using
`ggplot2`.

1.  A **data frame** containing your already tidy data.
2.  A **`ggplot` object**. This is initialized using the `ggplot` function.
3.  An **aesthetic mapping** indicates what role a variable plays in the plot. 
    -   Which variable (if any) is plotted on the $x$-axis? Which variable (if any) is plotted on the $y$-axis?
    - Which variable controls the color of features?
    - Which variable controls the size of features?
4.  A **geometric object**. These are called *geoms* for short.
    -   They indicate the type of plot that is desired.
    -   Histogram, density, boxplot, are some common examples of geoms.
        shape.
    -   They also indicate the geometric object used to visualize the data.
    -   Points, lines, or polygons are some examples of geoms to name a few.

In [*R for Data Science*](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-visualize), Wickham and Grolemund (2023) provide the following template for creating graphics using `ggplot2`:

```
ggplot(
  data = <DATA>,
  mapping = aes(<MAPPINGS>)
  ) +
  <GEOM_FUNCTION>()
```

`<DATA>`, `<MAPPINGS>`, and `<GEOM_FUNCTION>` are placeholders that you
replace with the data frame, aesthetic mappings, and geometric object, respectively, you want to use in your specific plot.

<br>

Sources:

- Wilkinson L (2005). *The grammar of graphics*. Statistics and computing, 2nd edn. Springer, New York
- Wickham (2010). *A layered grammar of graphics*. J Comput Graph Stat 19(1):3-28


## Basic Steps for Creating a Plot with `ggplot2`

---

Here is an explanation of the template above:

1.  Every `ggplot` starts with a call to the `ggplot` function.

2.  Generally, you pass your data frame to the `ggplot` through the
    `data` argument.
    -   You can also pass `data` inside the `<GEOM_FUNCTION>` when you intend to use multiple geometric objects with different data sources.


```{r}
# passing data into a ggplot to create an empty graph
ggplot(data = hawks)
```

3. `<MAPPINGS>` describes the aesthetics mappings you want to use for this particular geometry.
    - Generally, you pass your `<MAPPINGS>` to the `ggplot` through the `mappings` argument of `ggplot`.
    - You can also choose to pass your `<MAPPINGS>`through the `<GEOM_FUNCTION>`.


```{r}
# the x and y arguments of aes() specify
# which variables to map to the x and y axes.
ggplot(
  data = hawks,
  mapping = aes(x = wing, y = tail)
  )
```

4.  The `+` symbol is used to add a layer to your graphic.
    -   If your code spans multiple lines, then you need to make sure all lines but the last end with the `+` operator to stack the layers properly.

5.  The `<GEOM_FUNCTION>` indicates the geometric object you want to use in the plot.
    -   One of the reasons `ggplot2` is so powerful is that you can use different mappings for different geometric objects.


```{r}
# geom_point() adds a layer of points to your plot which creates a scatter plot
ggplot(
  data = hawks,
  mapping = aes(x = wing, y = tail)
) +
  geom_point()
```

We typically truncate the code by not explicitly stating the argument names.

```{r}
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = wing, y = tail)) +  # enter data and mappings
  geom_point()  # add geom layer
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Notice a warning about a row with missing values. This is a warning of a potential issue about the data we may want to investigate further. This is not an error message. The code ran perfectly fine and generated the intended plot. If the warnings distract you, then we can add an argument `na.rm = TRUE` in the `geom` layer or we can disable the warning using the code chunk option `#| warning: false`. Both are illustrated below. So as not to complicate the code, we tend to use the code chunk option `#| warning: false` to hide the warning rather than add the `na.rm = TRUE` argument to the code.
:::

```{r}
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = wing, y = tail)) +  
  geom_point(na.rm = TRUE)  # use argument to remove observations before plotting
```

```{r}
#| warning: false 
# the code chunk option `#| warning: false` disables warning
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = wing, y = tail)) +  
  geom_point()  # no longer need to use na.rm = TRUE
```


6.  We can account for additional potential lurking variables such as `age` or `species` by layering additional **aesthetics** onto our plot and see if they reveal any additional patterns or insight.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = wing, 
                  y = tail, 
                  color = species,  # include color aesthetic
                  shape = age)) +  # include shape aesthetic
  geom_point()  # add geom layer
```

7. Customize additional formatting layers.
  - Adjust the scale for the ticks on both axes.
  - Add a title, subtitle, and $x$-axis label.
  - Remove the gray paneling in the background, but keep the grid lines.
  - Move the legend below the graph, and increase the font size.

Below is an example of how we can store a foundation and then add layers to customize the plot.

```{r}
#| warning: false
# no output generated since we have
# stored previous plot to gghawk
gghawk <- ggplot(hawks, aes(x = wing, 
                            y = tail, 
                            color = species,  # include color aesthetic
                            shape = age)) +  # include shape aesthetic
  geom_point()  # add geom layer
```


```{r}
#| warning: false
gghawk + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 500, by = 50)) +  # customize scale on x-axis
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 300, by = 50)) +  # customize scale on y-axis
  labs(  # customize labels
    title = "Association Between Wing and Tail Measurements",
    subtitle = "Hawks",
    x = "Wing Length (in mm)",
    y = "Tail Length (in mm)") + 
  theme_light()  # use a custom theme
```

::: {.callout-note}
A `theme` is a customized style that changes the overall appearance of our graphic in non-data related ways.`ggplot2` provides a number of built-in themes. Some of the built-in themes include:

-   `theme_gray`: The default theme. Gray background and white grid lines.
-   `theme_bw`: White background and gray grid lines.
-   `theme_classic`: White background and no grid lines.
-   `theme_minimal`: White background, no grid lines, no axis lines.
-   `theme_light`: White background, gray grid lines, and a box around the plotting region.
:::

## Common Geoms

---

There are many geometric objects available in **ggplot2**. A complete
list may be (currently) found at <https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/>. A partial list of geometric objects that are frequently used are found below.


| dimensionality | geometry | purpose  |
|----------------|----------|----------|
| 1d | `geom_bar` | Draws a bar chart.  |
| 1d | `geom_density` | Draws a density plot. |
| 1d | `geom_histogram`    | Draws a histogram. |
| 1d | `geom_boxplot`  | Draws a boxplot.  |
| 1d | `geom_violin`   | Draws a violin plot.  |
| 1d | `geom_qq`       | Draws a quantile-quantile plot.  |
| 2d | `geom_point`    | Draws points. Used for scatter plots.  |
| 2d | `geom_path`, `geom_line` | Connects observations. Used for line plots. |
| 2d | `geom_segment`  | Draws straight lines between points.  |
| 2d | `geom_curve`    | Draws curved lines between points.  |
| 2d | `geom_smooth`   | Draws a ‘smooth’ fitted model of the data. |
| 2d | `geom_density2d`  | Draws 2d contours of density estimate for two variables.  |
| 2d  | `geom_density2d_filled` | Draws 2d contours of density estimate for two variables with colors. |
| 3d | `geom_contour`  | Draws 2d contours of 3d data. |
| 3d | `geom_contour_filled`  | Draws 2d contours of 3d data (colored). |
| NA | `geom_abline`, `geom_hline`, `geom_vline` | Draws diagonal, horizontal, and vertical lines. |

## Common Aesthetics

---

Aesthetic mappings are unique to each geometric object. Some of the most
common ones that show up in many geoms are provided below.

| aesthetic | purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| `x` | Controls the x-variable in the plot. |
| `y` | Controls the y-variable in the plot. |
| `alpha` | Controls the transparency of the object. |
| `color`, `colour` | Controls the colors of the object. |
| `fill` | Controls the color of the interior of an object. |
| `group` | Controls how the data are grouped. |
| `linetype` | Controls the type of line used to draw the object. |
| `size` | Controls the size of the drawn object. |
| `shape` | Controls the shape of the object. |


## Bar Plots with `geom_bar`

---

- Use the `geom_bar()` to construct bar plots.
- No variable is mapped to the `fill` aesthetic in the `geom_bar()`. 
  - Instead we map a fixed color to the `fill` aesthetic.
  - This changes the appearance of the plot.
  - But no additional features of the data are highlighted.


```{r}
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = species)) +  # plot factor variable species on x
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue")  # use the same fill color for all bars
```

- If we map `species` to the `fill` aesthetic, then each bar is plotted in a different color.
  - That might look nice? Maybe not your style?
  - Since the same variable is mapped to both aesthetics, we gain no new information from the colors.


```{r}
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = species, fill = species)) +  # use diff color for diff species
  geom_bar()
```


- If we map a different factor variable, such as `age` to the `fill` aesthetic, then we do gain additional information.
- The result is a stacked frequency bar chart.


```{r}
# mapping a second variable to a second aesthetic conveys additional info
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = species, fill = age)) + 
  geom_bar()
```

```{r}
# swapping variables and aesthetics results in different plot
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = age, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar()
```

```{r}
# we add additional layers for improved layout
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = age, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Age by Species",  # add main title
    x = "Species", y = "Count"   # add label on each axis
  ) + 
  theme_classic()
```


## Histograms with `geom_hist`

---

Use `geom_histogram()` to construct a histogram for a `numeric` variable that is mapped to the `x` aesthetic.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = culmen)) +
  geom_histogram()
```

- We can add additional options to customize `geom_histogram()`.
- Run `?geom_histogram` to access help documentation to view other available arguments.


```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = culmen)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 2,  # sets width of each bin to 2 mm
    fill = "steelblue",  # set fill color to steelblue
    color = "black"  # set outline color to black
    )
```


## Density Plots with `geom_density`

---

Use `geom_density()` to construct a density plot for a `numeric` variable that is mapped to the `x` aesthetic.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = culmen)) +
  geom_density()
```

- We can map other variables to other aesthetics to search for other lurking relations.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = culmen, color = species)) +
  geom_density()
```

- Since some people may not perceive colors as well as others, we can map a single variable to multiple aesthetics to communicate a relation using multiple modes such as `color` and `linetype`.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = culmen, 
                  color = species,
                  linetype = species)) +
  geom_density()
```

- Some aesthetics may work better than others. Beauty is in the eye of the beholder. Express yourself through the language of `ggplot2` aesthetics.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = culmen, 
                  fill = species)) +
  geom_density()
```

### Adjusting Transparency with `alpha`

---

To address masking issues, we can control the transparency of the colors using the `alpha` aesthetic. 

- `0` means completely transparent (not visible),
- `1` means completely opaque (cannot see anything behind it).

In the code cell below we set `alpha = 0.3`. Notice that we specify this in the `geom` layer, not in the  aesthetic mapping, since we want to apply the same value to all density plots.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = culmen, 
                  fill = species)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3)  # add alpha aesthetic here
```

## Box Plots with `geom_boxplot`

---

Use `geom_boxplot()` to construct a box plot of a `numeric` variable mapped to the `x` aesthetic.


```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = culmen)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

- We can always add additional layers for formatting and layout after working out how to convey important features and patterns in the data.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = culmen)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") +  # set fill color to steelblue
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = fivenum(hawks$culmen)) +  # customize ticks on x-axis
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Hawk Culmen Lengths", 
    x = "Culmen Length (in mm)",  
  ) +
  theme_bw() +  # use custom theme
  theme(
    axis.ticks.y=element_blank(),  # turn off y-axis ticks
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),  # remove minor gridlines
    panel.grid.major = element_blank())  # remove major gridlines
```

## Side-by-Side Boxplots with `geom_boxplot`

---

We can create side by side box plots by simply adding a categorical variable such as `species` to the opposite axis as the one the numeric variable is mapped to. In addition, a `fill` color to the box plots might be a more visually appealing graphic.


```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = species, y = culmen, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")  # legend adds no new info in this case 
```

## Violin Plots with `geom_violin`

---

A **violin plot** blends a box plot and a density plot. A violin plot unites a density with its mirror image and then displays the unified object like a box plot. Use `geom_violin()` to construct a violin plot for a `numeric` variable.


```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = species, y = culmen, fill = species)) +
  geom_violin() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")  # legend adds no new info in this case 
```


## Adding Smoothers to Scatter Plots

---

A **smoother** in `ggplot2` is a model that that attempts to estimate the average relationship between a response variable (typically the `y` variable) and one or more predictor variables (typically the `x` and possibly other variables).

- A smoothing layer can be added to a plot using `geom_smooth`.
- Adding a smoother to a plot can make relationships between variables even clearer.
- A pointwise confidence interval is shaded in gray by default to include an assessment of uncertainty.
  - We can turn off with confidence interval shading with the option `geom_smooth(se = FALSE)`.

There are many different models we can choose for the smoothing `method`. `ggplot2` takes the methods:

  - `lm` (linear model),
  - `glm` (generalized linear model),
  - `gam` (generalized additive model),
  - `loess` (local fitting),
  - or a function (e.g., `MASS::rlm` for a robust linear model).
  
If we do not know what these are but think they sound fancy, we should not add them to our plot. If we do not understand what we are adding to our plot, then it is not going to help us understand the data! Run the code cell below to open the help documentation for `geom_smooth()` for further information.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = tail, y = wing, color = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

```{r}
#| warning: false
# turn off conf int band with se = FALSE argument
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = tail, y = wing, color = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

## Adjusting Color Palette for Colorblind-Friendly Plots

---

We can improve the color palette to be more colorblind-friendly with the [`scale_color_colorblind()`](https://jrnold.github.io/ggthemes/reference/colorblind.html) function from the `ggthemes` package.

::: {.callout-warning}
If you have not already install the `ggthemes` package, you will need to first run the command `install.packages("ggthemes")` from the console below.
:::


```{r}
#| warning: false
#library(ggthemes)  # loaded in first code cell
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = tail, y = wing, color = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_color_colorblind() + # adjust color palette
  theme_bw()
```

## Local vs. Global Aesthetic Mappings

---

In `ggplot2`, there are two ways to map a variable to an aesthetic:

- A **global aesthetic mapping** applies across all geoms and is specified in the `ggplot` function

- A **local aesthetic mapping** is specified in a specific geom function and only applies to that particular geom.

In the plot above, we applied a global aesthetic mapping to the `species` variable using the `color` aesthetic to obtain three separate linear models for each of the three different species, resulting in a more complete picture.

In the code cell below, we use a local aesthetic mapping to produce a simpler version of the previous plot. This only adds a single line across all groups, which does not explain the relationship between body mass and bill length as well since it does not account for the confounding variable `species`.


```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = tail, y = wing)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species, shape = species), size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  scale_color_colorblind() + # adjust color palette
  theme_bw()
```

## Faceting

---

**Faceting** a `ggplot` creates separate plotting panels for each level of one or more categorical variables. Faceting creates arrays of plots by subsetting and displaying the same graph for each subset of the data.  Technically, faceting can be performed for discrete `numeric` variables with a relatively small number of unique values, but for practical reasons, faceting is most appropriate for `factor` variables.

There are two functions for creating faceted graphics in `ggplot2`:

- `facet_wrap` facets the plots based on a single `factor` variable. The panels are wrapped around the plotting window.
  - Wrapped is typically the more useful type of faceting.
- `facet_grid` forms a matrix of panels based on row and column faceting variables.

### Wrapped Faceting

---

In the plot below, we facet scatter plots of `wing` versus `tail` by `species`, and in addition we change the color of points to indicate the age group.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = wing, y = tail, color = age)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~species) + 
  scale_color_colorblind() + # adjust color palette
  theme_bw()
```

### Grid Faceting

---

We now explore the `facet_grid` function to facet by the `factor` variables `species` and `age`.  

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggplot(hawks, aes(x = wing, y = tail)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(species ~ age)
```

## Question 11

---

Clean up any issues you see with the data.

### Solution to Question 11

---

- Variable names are already good.
- `NA` values seem to be coded properly.
- The data type of some variables need to be converted.
  - Each conversion is explained in the comments in the code below.
  
```{r}
# convert from character to factor
# note status is already a factor data type
storms$name <- factor(storms$name)
storms$name <- factor(storms$name)
storms$category <- factor(storms$category)

# convert from double to integer
storms$year <- as.integer(storms$year)
storms$month <- as.integer(storms$month)
storms$day <- as.integer(storms$day)
storms$hour <- as.integer(storms$hour)
```


::: {.callout-note}
Some numeric variables such as `wind` and `pressure` (and others) are stored as `integer` even though they can be measured as a continuous numeric and stored as a decimal. The values are integers due to measurement limitations, so we'll just leave them as integers.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
We could leave `year`, `day`, `month`, `hour` as `double`, we can convert to `factor` or we can convert to `integer`. It depends on our goal. We choose integer data types since they might be sometimes treated as `numeric` by some functions when it makes sense (such as `mean()`, `median()`, `hist()`) and they can also be treated as an ordinal categorical variables with integers as the names for the levels, in which case functions like `table()` and aesthetic mapping in `ggplot2` work well.
:::


```{r}
# compute median of integer
median(storms$month)
```


```{r}
# count number of observations with each integer value
table(storms$month)
```

```{r}
# make sure data looks good
glimpse(storms)
```

<br>  
<br>  

:::{.callout-note}
For the remaining questions:

- Numeric variables to choose from are `year`, `month`, `day`, `hour`, `lat`, `long`, `wind`, `pressure`, `tropical_force_diameter`, and `hurricane_force_diamter`.
- Categorical variables are `name`, `status` and `category`.
- Integer data types such as `year`, `month`, `day`, and `hour` might also be treated as categorical variables in plots.
:::

## Question 13

---

Create one univariate plot for a categorical variable in `storms` using any method you prefer.


### Solution to Question 13

---

#### Base R Graphics Without Defaults

```{r}
# using generic plot function with factor results in bar plot
plot(storms$category)
```

```{r}
# using table and barplot base R to create bar plot
my_tbl <- table(storms$category)
barplot(my_tbl)
```


```{r}
# using prop.table to create relative freq bar plot
my_prop_tbl <- prop.table(table(storms$category))
barplot(my_prop_tbl)
```

#### `ggplot2` with Defaults

```{r}
# by default NA observations are included
# not what we want for this plot
ggplot(storms, aes(x = category)) + 
  geom_bar()  # geom for bar plot
```


```{r}
# a better plot when removing NA bar
# filter out obs with category not equal to NA
clean_category <- filter(storms, !is.na(category))
      
ggplot(clean_category, aes(x = category)) + 
  geom_bar()  # geom for bar plot
```

#### Base R with Additional Formatting

```{r}
# a frequency bar plot with nice format
plot(storms$category, 
     main = "Distribution of Hurricanes by Category",  # main title
     xlab = "Category Hurricane",  # title on x-axis
     ylab = "Count",  # title on y-axis
     col = rainbow(5))  # fill colors
```


```{r}
# a relative frequency bar plot with nice format
barplot(prop.table(table(storms$category)), 
     main = "Distribution of Hurricanes by Category",  # main title
     xlab = "Category Hurricane",  # title on x-axis
     ylab = "Proportion",  # title on y-axis
     col = terrain.colors(5))  # fill colors
```

```{r}
#| message: false
# bar plot with ggplot2 and improved layout
clean_category <- filter(storms, !is.na(category))  # filter out obs with category not equal to NA

ggplot(clean_category, aes(x = category)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Hurricane Category",  # add main title
    x = "Category", y = "Count"   # add label on each axis
  ) + 
  theme_classic()
```

## Question 14

Create a scatter plot to see whether there is a relation between two `numeric` variables in `storms`.

#### Base R Graphics Without Defaults

```{r}
# ggplot2 with no formatting
```

```{r}

```




#### `ggplot2` with Defaults


```{r}
     main = "Distribution of Wind Speeds by Status",  # main title
```

```{r}
     main = "Distribution of Wind Speeds by Status",  # main title

     ylab = "Wind Speed (in knots)",  # title on y-axis

     las = 3)  # rotate the labels on x axos
```

#### `ggplot2` with Formatting Options and Layers

```{r}
# ggplot2 with formatting changes
# better customization
ggplot(storms, aes(x = status, y = wind, fill = status)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(  # customize labels
    title = "Distribution of Wind Speeds by Storm Status",
    subtitle = "North Atlantic Storms 1975-2022",
    x = "Storm Status",
    y = "Wind Speed (in knots)") + 
  theme_light() + 
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",  # adds legend on top which works!
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)  # custom rotate status labels
  )  
```       


```{r}
# ggplot2 with formatting changes
# just changed geom to violin
ggplot(storms, aes(x = status, y = wind, fill = status)) +
  geom_violin() +
  labs(  # customize labels
    title = "Distribution of Wind Speeds by Storm Status",
    subtitle = "North Atlantic Storms 1975-2022",
    x = "Storm Status",
    y = "Wind Speed (in knots)") + 
  theme_light() + 
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",  # adds legend on top which works!
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)  # custom rotate status labels
  )  
```

# Interactive Plots with `plotly`

---

Interactive graphics are visual displays that dynamically provide information to users based on the user interacting with the graphic. Some of the best packages for creating interactive graphics in R are:

-   [`plotly`](https://plotly.com/): provides functions to make `ggplot2` graphics interactive and a custom interface to the JavaScript library `plotly.js` inspired by the grammar of graphics. This is perhaps the best known interactive visualization library.
-   [`ggiraph`](https://davidgohel.github.io/ggiraph/): creates interactive `ggplot2` graphics using [`htmlwidgets`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rgl/index.html).
-   [`rgl`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rgl/index.html): provides functions for 3D interactive graphics using OpenGL or to various standard 3D file formats
-   [`shiny`](https://shiny.posit.co/): a package for creating interactive web apps.

If we are already familiar with `ggplot2`, then `plotly` is super convenient. The easiest way to create interactive graphics with `ggplot2` and `plotly` is to:

1.  Create a plot using `ggplot2`.
2.  Use the `ggplotly()` function from the `plotly` package to make the graphic interactive.

That's it. We now can make just about any `ggplot2` plot interactive.

::: {.callout-warning}
If you have not already install the `plotly` package, you will need to first run the command `install.packages("plotly")` from the console below.
:::


## Interactive Bar Plots

---


1. Use `ggplot2` to create a basic bar plot of hawk `species`.
2. Use the `ggplotly()` function to convert the static `ggplot` to an interactive plot


::: {.callout-warning}
If you have not already install the `plotly` package, you will need to first run the command `install.packages("plotly")` from the console below. The `plotly` package is loaded in the first code cell of this document. If you have not run that code cell, be sure to run the command `library(plotly)` to load the package before running the code cell below.
:::

```{r}
# first create and store ggplot bar plot
#library(plotly)
ggbar <- ggplot(hawks, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar()

# then input into ggplotly to make it interactive
ggplotly(ggbar)
```



## Interactive Histograms

---

First create a histogram with `geom_histogram()`. Then input into `ggplotly()`. Scroll around the plot and use the tool bar on top to interact with the plot.


```{r}
#| warning: false
gghist <- ggplot(hawks, aes(x = culmen)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20)

ggplotly(gghist)
```


## Interactive Density Plots

---

First create a density plot with `geom_density()`. Then input into `ggplotly()`. Scroll around the plot and use the tool bar on top to interact with the plot.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggdens <- ggplot(hawks, aes(x = culmen, fill = species)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3)

ggplotly(ggdens)
```


## Interactive Box Plots

---

First create a box plot with `geom_boxplot()`. Then input into `ggplotly()`. Scroll around the plot and use the tool bar on top to interact with the plot.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggbox <- ggplot(hawks, aes(x = species, y = culmen)) +
  geom_boxplot()
ggplotly(ggbox)
```

## Interactive Scatter Plots

---

First create a scatter plot with `geom_point()`. Then input into `ggplotly()`. Scroll around the plot and use the tool bar on top to interact with the plot.

```{r}
ggscatter <-
  ggplot(hawks, 
         aes(x = wing,
             y = tail,
             color = species,
             shape = species)) +
  geom_point()
ggplotly(ggscatter)
```


Notice that `species` is indicated twice when we hover over a point.
We can correct this behavior by using the `tooltip` argument to specify the attributes (`x`, `y`, `color`, etc.) we want to display when our mouse hovers over a point.

```{r}
# restrict attributes displayed from hover
ggplotly(ggscatter,
         tooltip = c("shape", "x", "y"))
```

## Adding Smooths to an Interactive Scatter Plot Using `ggplot2` and `ggplotly()`

---

In the code below, we:

1.  Use `ggplot2` to create a scatter plot of `wing` versus `tail` that uses different colors and shapes to distinguish the different `species`.
2.  Add a second layer to the plot the provides an `"lm"` smooth for the points of each `species`. We assign this plot the name `ggsmooth`.
3.  Use `plotly::ggplotly` to make the graphic interactive.

The interactive graphic indicates the `species`, `wing`, and `tail` of each point, points on the .

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
ggsmooth <- ggplot(hawks, aes(x = wing,
                              y = tail,
                              color = species,
                              shape = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

ggplotly(ggsmooth)
```


# Appendix: Color Palettes Available with `base` R

---

```{r}
#| echo: false
require("graphics")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

## color swatches for RGB/HSV palettes
demo.pal <-
  function(n, border = if (n < 32) "light gray" else NA,
           main = paste("color palettes;  n=", n),
           ch.col = c("rainbow(n, start=.7, end=.1)", 
                      "heat.colors(n)",
                      "terrain.colors(n)", "topo.colors(n)",
                      "cm.colors(n)")) {
    nt <- length(ch.col)
    i <- 1:n; j <- n / nt; d <- j/6; dy <- 2*d
    plot(i, i+d, type = "n", yaxt = "n", ylab = "", main = main)
    for (k in 1:nt) {
        rect(i-.5, (k-1)*j+ dy, i+.4, k*j,
             col = eval(str2lang(ch.col[k])), border = border)
        text(2*j,  k * j + dy/4, ch.col[k])
    }
}
demo.pal(16)
```


# Appendix: Color Swatches for HCL Palettes

---

```{r}
#| echo: false
## color swatches for HCL palettes
hcl.swatch <- function(type = NULL, n = 5, nrow = 4,
  border = if (n < 15) "black" else NA) {
    palette <- hcl.pals(type)
    cols <- sapply(palette, hcl.colors, n = n)
    ncol <- ncol(cols)
    nswatch <- min(ncol, nrow)

    par(mar = rep(0.1, 4),
        mfrow = c(1, min(5, ceiling(ncol/nrow))),
        pin = c(1, 0.5 * nswatch),
        cex = 0.7)

    while (length(palette)) {
        subset <- 1:min(nrow, ncol(cols))
        plot.new()
        plot.window(c(0, n), c(0, nrow + 1))
        text(0, rev(subset) + 0.1, palette[subset], adj = c(0, 0))
        y <- rep(subset, each = n)
        rect(rep(0:(n-1), n), rev(y), rep(1:n, n), rev(y) - 0.5,
             col = cols[, subset], border = border)
        palette <- palette[-subset]
        cols <- cols[, -subset, drop = FALSE]
    }

    par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 4.1, 2.1), cex = 1)
}

hcl.swatch("qualitative")
hcl.swatch("sequential")
hcl.swatch("diverging")
hcl.swatch("divergingx")
```
